Sage.et: From Middle High German sage, from Old High German saga, from Proto-West Germanic *sagā, from Proto-Germanic *sagǭ.

Säge.et:
From Middle High German sage, from Old High German saga, from Proto-West Germanic *sagu, from Proto-Germanic *sagō, from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”).

sagen.et: From Middle High German sagen, from Old High German sagēn, from Proto-West Germanic *saggjan, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ-. Cognate with Bavarian sogn, Alemannic German säge, Low German seggen, Dutch zeggen, English …

sägen.et: From Middle High German segen, sagen, from Old High German segōn, sagōn. Equivalent to Säge + -en. The two vocalic forms are considered ablaut variants, not umlaut variants; the spelling with -ä- is a compromise form.

s: legendary, mythical (of or pertaining to a legend (myth) or saga)
Die sagenhafte Gründung Roms fand 753 vor Christi statt.
mythical, storied (known chiefly through stories, and hence perhaps of dubious reality)
sagenhaft.et: 19th c., Sage + -n- + haft. Compare similar Middle High German sagehaft (“which is spoken of, famous”) which was not continued.

s: Einer sagt ein Wort und die andern müssen es zeichnen, und der Sager wählt dann die beste Zeichnung aus.
Someone says a word and the others must draw it, and then the sayer chooses the best drawing.

Sägemehl.et: From sägen (“to saw”) + Mehl (“flour”). The loss of the final -n is regular in compounds from verb stems. Alternatively analysable as Säge (“a saw”) + Mehl.

s: legendary, shrouded in myth (the subject of many legends, mysticized)

sago (powdered starch obtained from certain palms)
a whopping, no less than, believe it or not (emphasizes the scale of a number)
Durch jahrelange Arbeit hat sie sage und schreibe drei Millionen Euro angesammelt.
Through years of work, she has accumulated a whopping three million Euros.
used to indicate that one is missing a word and to invite the collocutor to fill it in
Ich hatte doch diesen... ach, sag schnell... diesen Meniskusriss.
You know I had this... ah, you know what... this torn meniscus.
a thin shaving or chip of wood produced during sawing
Sägespan.et: Equivalent to Säge or sägen + Span; ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sagōspēnuz. Compare Plautdietsch Soagespoon n, Swedish sågspån, Faroese saguspønir m pl (“sawdust”).
